h1:
Than Ngam Waterfall
Forest, Rock Flats & Rainy-Season Water
intro: Than Ngam Waterfall sits deep in the Phu Phan forest in Nong Saeng district, about 50 kilometres south of Udon Thani town. It's the kind of nature spot locals like to drive out to in the rainy season, because that's when the water runs hardest, spilling down the rock pools in tiers. It's less than half a kilometre on foot from the car park to the falls, and all around you'll find wide rock flats, dry dipterocarp forest, and a nature trail to wander through in the cool air. This isn't a huge, dramatic waterfall — it's a place you come to sit and listen to the water, soak your feet in a pool, and actually breathe with the forest.

blocks.html: Let's be straight from the start — Than Ngam isn't the tall, towering waterfall you see on posters. It's a low one that runs in steps down a series of rock flats. The charm is in the real forest, the quiet, and the clear cold water. Anyone expecting something dramatic might shrug, but if you want to escape town to sit and listen to water in the forest, soak your feet in a pool, and stroll across the rock flats, this place hits the spot — especially if you come in the right season.

blocks.text: Where Than Ngam Waterfall is and how to get there

blocks.html: Than Ngam Waterfall lies within Than Ngam Waterfall Forest Park in Tab Kung sub-district, Nong Saeng, in the south of the province — forest on the smaller Phu Phan Noi range. It's about 50 kilometres from Udon Thani town, roughly an hour's drive. The final stretch climbs a little into the hills, but a regular sedan handles it fine. Once you reach the forest park you park up and walk in another 300–400 metres to the falls. It's neither far nor steep, so kids and older walkers can manage it.

items: Location — Than Ngam Waterfall Forest Park, Tab Kung sub-district, Nong Saeng, Udon Thani
Distance — about 50 km from Udon Thani town, roughly a 1-hour drive
Walk in — about 300–400 metres on foot from the car park to the falls
Getting there — best with your own car or a rental; public transport doesn't reach it

blocks.title: Pair it with Phu Foi Lom
blocks.html: Than Ngam is in the same zone as Phu Foi Lom Park, so most people roll the two into a single day. Walk the Than Ngam falls in the morning, head up to Phu Foi Lom in the afternoon for the botanical gardens and cooler air, and you're back in town in time for dinner. It's the neatest nature route in the south of the province.

blocks.text: The rainy season is when the water runs strongest and looks best

blocks.html: Than Ngam has water running almost year-round, but the time it truly runs hard and fills the pools is the rainy season, roughly June to November. Rain on the Phu Phan hills feeds the stream until the falls flow strong, the water turns clear, and the pools get deep enough to swim in — and the forest all around is at its greenest. If you come in the dry months around March and April, the water drops so low that some spots are just a trickle and you can't really swim. So if your plan is to get in the water, aim for the rainy season or early winter just after the rains end, while there's still plenty of flow.

The thing to watch in the rainy season is that after heavy rain, flash water can come down faster and harder than usual, and the rocks along the falls get very slippery. If you see the water turning muddy or flowing unusually fast, don't push it — sit and watch from the bank, it's safer. And don't leave your things near the water's edge, because the level rises quickly.

blocks.text: Rock flats, dipterocarp forest, and the trails

blocks.html: Beyond the falls themselves, what makes Than Ngam worth wandering is the wide sandstone flats scattered across several spots in the forest park. Some are open expanses of rock for walking and photos; others have water running over them as low rapids. Around them is dry dipterocarp forest mixed with evergreen — open underfoot and easy to walk, lush and shaded in the rains. In late winter and early summer, the dipterocarp leaves turn and drop, carpeting the ground a reddish brown — a completely different mood.

items.name: The main Than Ngam falls
items.blurb: A low waterfall stepping down the rock flats in tiers, with shallow pools to soak your feet and wade. This is the main spot where most people stop.

items.name: Wide rock flats
items.blurb: Open sandstone flats around the forest park — good for photos and a rest, with water running over some of them as low rapids.

items.name: Dipterocarp & evergreen forest
items.blurb: Open, easy-walking forest — lush and green in the rains, and a reddish-brown carpet of fallen dipterocarp leaves in late winter.

items.name: Inner falls and caves
items.blurb: Deeper in the forest are inner-tier falls like Tad Makha and Wang Tad Phae, plus caves. These need a longer walk and a ranger guide.

blocks.title: Want to go deeper? Check with the rangers first
blocks.html: The main falls are easy to reach on your own, but if you want to push on to the inner falls or caves deeper in the forest, stop and ask the forest-park rangers about the route and safety first. Some trails need a guide. Don't head deep into the forest alone without telling anyone — especially in the rainy season when the paths are slick and flash water comes fast.

blocks.text: Opening hours, parking fee, and what to know

blocks.html: The forest park is open during daylight, roughly 08:00–17:00. It's set up for day trips — go in the morning, back by evening — not for convenient overnight stays. There's no formal entrance fee for the falls, just a parking charge of around 20 THB. Around the car park there are a few local food and drink stalls, but not many, so it's worth bringing some water and snacks of your own.

items: Opening hours — roughly 08:00–17:00, a morning-to-evening day trip
Parking fee — about 20 THB; no formal entrance fee for the falls
Footwear — wear non-slip shoes, as the rocks by the water are very slippery in the rains
Litter — carry it back to town to bin; help keep the forest for the next visitors

blocks.text: About Phu Phra Bat and the rock flats people mix up

blocks.html: Let's clear this up to avoid confusion: the words "rock flats" and the name Phu Phra Bat often get lumped together, but they're actually two different places. Than Ngam Waterfall and the rock flats described above are in Than Ngam Waterfall–Phu Foi Lom Forest Park, in Nong Saeng district in the south of the province. Phu Phra Bat Historical Park — the one with sandstone flats, oddly shaped stone pillars, and Dvaravati-era boundary stones that earned it World Heritage status — is in Ban Phue district, in a different direction and a fair distance away. Both have rock flats, but they're separate sites. If you're set on seeing the World Heritage stone pillars, you need Ban Phue, not Nong Saeng.

faq.q: Which district is Than Ngam Waterfall in, and is it far from Udon Thani town?
faq.a: It's in Than Ngam Waterfall Forest Park, Tab Kung sub-district, Nong Saeng, in the south of the province, about 50 kilometres from Udon Thani town — roughly an hour's drive. Once you reach the forest park you park up and walk in another 300–400 metres to the falls.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Than Ngam Waterfall for the best water?
faq.a: The rainy season from June to November is when the water runs strongest and the pools fill up, so you can swim properly and the forest around is lush. Early winter, just after the rains end, still has plenty of flow too. In the dry months around March and April the water drops so low that some spots are just a trickle and you can't really swim.

faq.q: Is there an entrance fee for Than Ngam Waterfall, and what time does it open?
faq.a: The forest park is open during daylight, roughly 08:00–17:00. There's no formal entrance fee for the falls, just a parking charge of around 20 THB. There are a few local food stalls near the car park, but it's best to bring your own water.

faq.q: Can you swim at Than Ngam Waterfall, and is it dangerous?
faq.a: You can swim in the shallow pools when the water is at a normal level, but in the rainy season after heavy rain, flash water can come fast and hard, and the rocks by the water are very slippery. If you see the water turning muddy or flowing unusually fast, get up onto the bank to watch and don't push it — and don't leave your things near the water's edge, because the level rises quickly.

faq.q: Are Than Ngam Waterfall and the Phu Phra Bat rock flats the same place?
faq.a: They're different places. Than Ngam Waterfall and its rock flats are in Than Ngam Waterfall–Phu Foi Lom Forest Park, Nong Saeng district, while Phu Phra Bat Historical Park — with its stone pillars and World Heritage boundary stones — is in Ban Phue district, in a different direction and a fair distance away. If you're set on seeing the World Heritage stone pillars, you need to go to Ban Phue.
